sections.title: 3 The Kernel Triple Formalism
sections.text: 3 The Kernel Triple Formalism The axiom of consent provides a static characterization of legitimacy: voice should track stakes, mediated by alignment and entropy. But governance is dynamic—configurations evolve, institutions transform, norms shift. How does friction change over time? Under what conditions do consent-respecting arrangements emerge, persist, or dissolve? To answer these questions, we require a dynamical treatment that maps the axiom’s core concepts onto evolutionary mechanics. This section introduces the kernel triple formalism —the mathematical apparatus connecting the axiom’s [LaTeX: (\alpha,\sigma,\varepsilon)] ( α , σ , ε ) (\alpha,\sigma,\varepsilon) structure to replicator-mutator dynamics via a scale-relative parameterization [LaTeX: (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S})] ( ρ S , w S , M S ) (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S}) [ 31 , 51 ] . The key insight is structural: the axiom’s alignment-stake-entropy triple instantiates directly into the survival-weight-mutation kernel governing type dynamics. Consent-respecting configurations are not imposed by fiat but emerge as attractors under selection pressure. 3.1 Motivation: From Statics to Dynamics The friction function (Eq. 6 ) characterizes tension at a point in time. But political reality is evolutionary: revolutionary movements gain adherents or dissipate; institutional reforms propagate or stall; governance norms spread or contract. A purely static framework cannot address the central question of political theory: why do some arrangements persist while others collapse? Three considerations motivate the dynamical extension: Temporal evolution. Friction is not constant. As stakes shift, information flows change, and alignments drift, the friction landscape transforms. A configuration that minimizes friction today may become untenable tomorrow. We require equations governing [LaTeX: \partial F/\partial t] ∂ F / ∂ t \partial F/\partial t . Types, not individuals. Political dynamics operate at multiple scales simultaneously. Individual preference changes matter, but so do institutional reforms, cultural shifts, and paradigm transitions. A statistical-mechanics approach—tracking distributions over types rather than individual trajectories—provides the appropriate level of abstraction. This parallels the move from Newtonian mechanics (individual trajectories) to thermodynamics (ensemble distributions) in physics. Scale-relativity. Different observables become relevant at different resolutions. The voter and the polity occupy different scales; describing both requires scale-relative primitives. The atomic unit itself must become a parameter, not a fixed assumption. 3.2 The Scale-Relative Kernel We formalize the notion of scale and the parameters defined relative to it. Definition 3.1 (Scale) . A scale [LaTeX: S] S S specifies: (i) A type space [LaTeX: T_{S}] T S T_{S} —the set of distinguishable configurations at scale [LaTeX: S] S S (ii) An observable algebra [LaTeX: \mathcal{O}_{S}] 𝒪 S \mathcal{O}_{S} —the measurable quantities at scale [LaTeX: S] S S (iii) A resolution parameter [LaTeX: r_{S}>0] r S > 0 r_{S}>0 —the characteristic spatiotemporal granularity Scales are observer-relative measurement choices, not objective features of reality. The same system admits description at multiple scales, with different scales revealing different dynamics. At agent scale, the atomic unit is an intentional agent; at institutional scale, the atomic unit is an institution; at cultural scale, the atomic unit is a belief system or practice. Definition 3.2 (Atomic Agent) . Given scale [LaTeX: S] S S , the atomic agent [LaTeX: \text{Atom}_{S}] Atom S \text{Atom}_{S} is the minimal unit of analysis—the entity treated as indivisible for purposes of description at that scale. Atomicity is not ontological fundamentality but resolution-relative non-decomposition. This scale-relativity principle distinguishes the formalism from domain-specific applications. We are not claiming that “everything is selection” as metaphysics, but that many domains admit a selection-transmission description once one chooses appropriate scale-relative parameters. 3.3 The Triple [LaTeX: (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S})] ( ρ S , w S , M S ) (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S}) At each scale [LaTeX: S] S S , dynamics are governed by three functions constituting the kernel triple . Theorem 3.1 (Type Dynamics) . Given scale [LaTeX: S] S S with type space [LaTeX: T_{S}] T S T_{S} , kernel triple [LaTeX: (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S})] ( ρ S , w S , M S ) (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S}) , and population distribution [LaTeX: p_{t}\in\Delta(T_{S})] p t ∈ Δ ⁡ ( T S ) p_{t}\in\Delta(T_{S}) , the temporal evolution of type frequencies is: [LaTeX: \boxed{\frac{dp_{t}(\tau)}{dt}=\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\in T_{S}}p_{t}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot w_{S}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot\rho_{S}(\tau^{\prime},G_{S,t},p_{t})\cdot M_{S}(\tau^{\prime}\to\tau)-p_{t}(\tau)\cdot\bar{\phi}_{t}}] d ​ p t ​ ( τ ) d ​ t = ∑ τ ′ ∈ T S p t ​ ( τ ′ ) ⋅ w S ​ ( τ ′ ) ⋅ ρ S ​ ( τ ′ , G S , t , p t ) ⋅ M S ​ ( τ ′ → τ ) − p t ​ ( τ ) ⋅ ϕ ¯ t \boxed{\frac{dp_{t}(\tau)}{dt}=\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\in T_{S}}p_{t}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot w_{S}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot\rho_{S}(\tau^{\prime},G_{S,t},p_{t})\cdot M_{S}(\tau^{\prime}\to\tau)-p_{t}(\tau)\cdot\bar{\phi}_{t}} (10) where the mean fitness [LaTeX: \bar{\phi}_{t}=\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\in T_{S}}p_{t}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot w_{S}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot\rho_{S}(\tau^{\prime},G_{S,t},p_{t})] ϕ ¯ t = ∑ τ ′ ∈ T S p t ​ ( τ ′ ) ⋅ w S ​ ( τ ′ ) ⋅ ρ S ​ ( τ ′ , G S , t , p t ) \bar{\phi}_{t}=\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\in T_{S}}p_{t}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot w_{S}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot\rho_{S}(\tau^{\prime},G_{S,t},p_{t}) normalizes the dynamics, ensuring [LaTeX: \sum_{\tau}dp_{t}(\tau)/dt=0] ∑ τ d ​ p t ​ ( τ ) / d ​ t = 0 \sum_{\tau}dp_{t}(\tau)/dt=0 and preserving the probability simplex. The ROM equation is not novel—it is the weighted replicator-mutator equation, well-established in evolutionary game theory [ 28 , 53 ] . What is novel is the explicit kernel parameterization enabling systematic cross-domain instantiation, and the specific consent-friction instantiation we develop below. The second term removes the current proportion of [LaTeX: \tau] τ \tau at rate equal to mean fitness. Types with above-average effective fitness (product of weight, survival, and transmission to self) increase in frequency; those below average decrease. 3.5 Consent Instantiation: Mapping [LaTeX: (\alpha,\sigma,\varepsilon)] ( α , σ , ε ) (\alpha,\sigma,\varepsilon) to [LaTeX: (\rho,w,M)] ( ρ , w , M ) (\rho,w,M) The axiom of consent defines friction in terms of alignment ( [LaTeX: \alpha] α \alpha ), stake ( [LaTeX: \sigma] σ \sigma ), and entropy ( [LaTeX: \varepsilon] ε \varepsilon ). The kernel triple provides the dynamical scaffolding. The central theoretical contribution is establishing the structural correspondence between these formalisms. Definition 3.6 (Consent-Weighted Survival) . In the consent domain, the survival function takes the legitimacy-friction form : [LaTeX: \rho_{S}^{\text{consent}}(\tau,G,p)=\frac{L(\tau)}{1+F(\tau)}] ρ S consent ​ ( τ , G , p ) = L ⁡ ( τ ) 1 + F ⁡ ( τ ) \rho_{S}^{\text{consent}}(\tau,G,p)=\frac{L(\tau)}{1+F(\tau)} (11) where [LaTeX: L(\tau)] L ⁡ ( τ ) L(\tau) is the legitimacy of configuration [LaTeX: \tau] τ \tau (distributional match between stakes and voice) and [LaTeX: F(\tau)] F ⁡ ( τ ) F(\tau) is the friction generated by [LaTeX: \tau] τ \tau . This functional form ensures that survival increases with legitimacy and decreases with friction. Configurations with perfect legitimacy ( [LaTeX: L=1] L = 1 L=1 ) and zero friction ( [LaTeX: F=0] F = 0 F=0 ) achieve [LaTeX: \rho=1] ρ = 1 \rho=1 . Configurations with zero legitimacy achieve [LaTeX: \rho=0] ρ = 0 \rho=0 regardless of friction. The denominator [LaTeX: (1+F)] ( 1 + F ) (1+F) bounds survival probability appropriately. Definition 3.7 (Consent-Friction Mapping) . The axiom’s terms map to kernel components as follows: Axiom Term Kernel Term Interpretation [LaTeX: \alpha] α \alpha (alignment) Encoded in [LaTeX: \rho_{S}] ρ S \rho_{S} Higher alignment [LaTeX: \to] → \to higher survival; alignment enters friction function inversely, thus survival positively [LaTeX: \sigma] σ \sigma (stake) [LaTeX: w_{S}] w S w_{S} (weight) Stakes determine influence on dynamics; higher stakes [LaTeX: \to] → \to larger weight in evolutionary pressure [LaTeX: \varepsilon] ε \varepsilon (entropy) [LaTeX: M_{S}] M S M_{S} (mutation) Information loss as type transition probability; high entropy [LaTeX: \to] → \to increased transmission noise The correspondence is not metaphorical but structural. Alignment enters the survival function through friction: from Eq. 6 , [LaTeX: F\propto(1+\varepsilon)/(1+\alpha)] F ∝ ( 1 + ε ) / ( 1 + α ) F\propto(1+\varepsilon)/(1+\alpha) , so high alignment reduces friction and increases [LaTeX: \rho_{S}=L/(1+F)] ρ S = L / ( 1 + F ) \rho_{S}=L/(1+F) . Stakes operate as weights: configurations affecting high-stakes agents exert proportionally larger selection pressure. Entropy operates as mutation: information loss in consent transfers manifests as noisy transmission of institutional templates. 3.5.1 Stake as Weight The mapping [LaTeX: \sigma\mapsto w_{S}] σ ↦ w S \sigma\mapsto w_{S} requires elaboration. In the axiom, stakes [LaTeX: s_{i}(d)] s i ​ ( d ) s_{i}(d) quantify an agent’s sensitivity to outcomes in domain [LaTeX: d] d d . In the kernel formalism, weights [LaTeX: w_{S}(\tau)] w S ​ ( τ ) w_{S}(\tau) quantify a type’s baseline replication capacity. The connection operates through aggregation. For a configuration (type) [LaTeX: \tau] τ \tau representing a governance arrangement: [LaTeX: w_{S}(\tau)=\sum_{i\in\text{Stakeholders}(\tau)}s_{i}\cdot\mathbf{1}[\text{$i$ supports persistence of }\tau]] w S ​ ( τ ) = ∑ i ∈ Stakeholders ​ ( τ ) s i ⋅ 𝟏 ​ [ i supports persistence of ​ τ ] w_{S}(\tau)=\sum_{i\in\text{Stakeholders}(\tau)}s_{i}\cdot\mathbf{1}[\text{$i$ supports persistence of }\tau] (12) High-stakes stakeholders supporting an arrangement contribute more to its evolutionary weight. This captures the empirical observation that institutions with powerful supporters persist longer, ceteris paribus. The weight function thus aggregates individual stakes into type-level evolutionary advantage. 3.5.2 Entropy as Mutation The mapping [LaTeX: \varepsilon\mapsto M_{S}] ε ↦ M S \varepsilon\mapsto M_{S} captures how information loss affects institutional transmission. When consent-holders imperfectly understand delegator preferences (high [LaTeX: \varepsilon] ε \varepsilon ), the policies they implement diverge from intended outcomes. This divergence is structurally equivalent to mutation in transmission. High entropy increases off-diagonal elements (transitions away from [LaTeX: \tau^{\prime}] τ ′ \tau^{\prime} ), reflecting that information-impoverished configurations produce more transmission errors. After modulation, row-stochasticity must be restored: [LaTeX: M_{S}(\tau^{\prime}\to\tau)\leftarrow\frac{M_{S}(\tau^{\prime}\to\tau)}{\sum_{\tau^{\prime\prime}}M_{S}(\tau^{\prime}\to\tau^{\prime\prime})}] M S ​ ( τ ′ → τ ) ← M S ​ ( τ ′ → τ ) ∑ τ ′′ M S ​ ( τ ′ → τ ′′ ) M_{S}(\tau^{\prime}\to\tau)\leftarrow\frac{M_{S}(\tau^{\prime}\to\tau)}{\sum_{\tau^{\prime\prime}}M_{S}(\tau^{\prime}\to\tau^{\prime\prime})} (14) 3.5.3 Alignment as Survival Modulator Alignment enters survival through the friction function. Recall the friction function (Definition 2.4 ): [LaTeX: F(\tau)=\sum_{i\in A}s_{i}\cdot\frac{1+\varepsilon_{i}(\tau)}{1+\alpha_{i}(\tau)}] F ⁡ ( τ ) = ∑ i ∈ A s i ⋅ 1 + ε i ​ ( τ ) 1 + α i ​ ( τ ) F(\tau)=\sum_{i\in A}s_{i}\cdot\frac{1+\varepsilon_{i}(\tau)}{1+\alpha_{i}(\tau)} (15) The inverse dependence on alignment ensures that configurations with high consent-holder/stakeholder alignment generate lower friction and thus higher survival probability. We can express this modulation explicitly: [LaTeX: \rho_{S}^{\text{consent}}(\tau)=\rho_{S}^{\text{base}}(\tau)\cdot\exp\left(-\lambda\cdot F(\tau)\right)] ρ S consent ( τ ) = ρ S base ( τ ) ⋅ exp ( − λ ⋅ F ( τ ) ) \rho_{S}^{\text{consent}}(\tau)=\rho_{S}^{\text{base}}(\tau)\cdot\exp\left(-\lambda\cdot F(\tau)\right) (16) where [LaTeX: \rho_{S}^{\text{base}}] ρ S base \rho_{S}^{\text{base}} is a baseline survival function and [LaTeX: \lambda>0] λ > 0 \lambda>0 scales friction’s effect. This exponential suppression form ensures: • [LaTeX: \rho_{S}>0] ρ S > 0 \rho_{S}>0 for all finite friction • [LaTeX: \rho_{S}\to 0] ρ S → 0 \rho_{S}\to 0 as friction diverges • Smooth interpolation between low and high friction regimes 3.6 The Unification: Isomorphism of Structure The central claim of this section is now statable precisely. Theorem 3.2 (Axiom-Kernel Correspondence) . The axiom of consent’s kernel triple [LaTeX: (\alpha,\sigma,\varepsilon)] ( α , σ , ε ) (\alpha,\sigma,\varepsilon) and the ROM kernel triple [LaTeX: (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S})] ( ρ S , w S , M S ) (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S}) are structurally isomorphic under the consent-friction instantiation. Specifically: (i) Alignment-Survival: [LaTeX: \alpha] α \alpha enters [LaTeX: \rho_{S}] ρ S \rho_{S} through the friction function; higher alignment yields higher survival probability via [LaTeX: \rho_{S}=L/(1+F)] ρ S = L / ( 1 + F ) \rho_{S}=L/(1+F) where [LaTeX: F\propto(1+\varepsilon)/(1+\alpha)] F ∝ ( 1 + ε ) / ( 1 + α ) F\propto(1+\varepsilon)/(1+\alpha) . (ii) Stake-Weight: [LaTeX: \sigma] σ \sigma determines [LaTeX: w_{S}] w S w_{S} ; aggregate stakes of supporting stakeholders constitute the type’s evolutionary weight. (iii) Entropy-Mutation: [LaTeX: \varepsilon] ε \varepsilon modulates [LaTeX: M_{S}] M S M_{S} ; information loss increases transmission noise, widening the mutation kernel’s dispersion. Proof sketch. The correspondence follows from the definitions. For (i): substituting [LaTeX: F=\sigma(1+\varepsilon)/(1+\alpha)] F = σ ⁡ ( 1 + ε ) / ( 1 + α ) F=\sigma(1+\varepsilon)/(1+\alpha) into [LaTeX: \rho_{S}=L/(1+F)] ρ S = L / ( 1 + F ) \rho_{S}=L/(1+F) yields survival as a function of alignment. For (ii): weighting type dynamics by stakeholder stakes is precisely the ROM weight function’s role. For (iii): entropy’s information-loss interpretation matches mutation’s imperfect-transmission interpretation; both increase variance in type production. The structural isomorphism holds because both formalisms decompose the same phenomenon—consent-weighted persistence—into the same three components, viewed from static (axiom) and dynamic (kernel) perspectives. ∎ This unification is the key theoretical contribution. It shows that the axiom of consent is not merely a normative principle but has dynamical implications: consent-aligned configurations are evolutionarily favored. “Ought” connects to “is” not through logical derivation but through selection: what persists is constrained by what generates less friction. 3.7 Properties of the Consent-Kernel Dynamics We now establish formal properties of the consent-friction instantiation. When an agent holds consent over a domain for extended periods, their subjective perception shifts from “holding consent for [LaTeX: d] d d ” toward “owning authority over [LaTeX: d] d d .” This psychological ownership accumulates over time and affects the mutation kernel. The Arrhenius-like exponential form ensures transitions remain possible but increasingly difficult with ownership accumulation. This generates the prediction that regime transition probability decreases exponentially with incumbent tenure—a testable distinction from generic “institutional stickiness” explanations. 3.9 Coarse-Graining and Scale Transitions The scale-relativity of the kernel triple raises the question of how dynamics at one scale relate to dynamics at another. The coarse-graining operator formalizes this relationship. Definition 3.10 (Coarse-Graining Operator) . For scales [LaTeX: S] S S (fine) and [LaTeX: S^{\prime}] S ′ S^{\prime} (coarse), the coarse-graining operator [LaTeX: \pi_{S\to S^{\prime}}:\Delta(T_{S})\to\Delta(T_{S^{\prime}})] π S → S ′ : Δ ⁡ ( T S ) → Δ ⁡ ( T S ′ ) \pi_{S\to S^{\prime}}:\Delta(T_{S})\to\Delta(T_{S^{\prime}}) maps fine-grained type distributions to coarse-grained distributions. This connects to the Mori-Zwanzig formalism in statistical mechanics [ 71 ] and explains why “emergence” appears mysterious: it is what coarse-graining looks like when lumpability conditions fail. 3.10 Summary: The Kernel Triple as Dynamical Backbone This section established the kernel triple formalism connecting the axiom of consent to evolutionary dynamics. The key results are: 1. Scale-relative parameterization: The kernel triple [LaTeX: (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S})] ( ρ S , w S , M S ) (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S}) provides domain-general apparatus for selection-transmission dynamics at any scale. 2. Consent instantiation: The axiom’s [LaTeX: (\alpha,\sigma,\varepsilon)] ( α , σ , ε ) (\alpha,\sigma,\varepsilon) maps structurally onto [LaTeX: (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S})] ( ρ S , w S , M S ) (\rho_{S},w_{S},M_{S}) via: • Alignment entering survival through the friction function • Stakes determining evolutionary weight • Entropy modulating the mutation kernel 3. Selection for consent: Consent-respecting configurations exhibit higher survival probability; friction acts as negative selection pressure. 4. The kernel triple provides the dynamical backbone for the axiom of consent. What remains is to examine its empirical implications (Section 6 ) and domain-specific applications (Section 5 ). sections.text: 4 Core Dynamics The kernel triple formalism established in Section 3 maps the axiom’s static characterization onto evolutionary mechanics. We now develop the full dynamical treatment: how friction evolves, how legitimacy changes, and what equilibrium properties emerge. The central result is that consent-respecting configurations are not normative ideals imposed from without but attractors under selection pressure—what persists is constrained by what generates less friction. 4.1 The ROM Equation: Generalized Replicator-Mutator Dynamics We begin by situating the ROM (Replicator-Optimization Mechanism) equation within the broader landscape of evolutionary dynamics, then establish its consent-specific instantiation. 4.1.1 Connection to Standard Replicator Dynamics The classical replicator equation [ 66 ] governs frequency dynamics in populations under selection: [LaTeX: \frac{dp_{t}(\tau)}{dt}=p_{t}(\tau)\left[\pi(\tau,p_{t})-\bar{\pi}(p_{t})\right]] d ​ p t ​ ( τ ) d ​ t = p t ​ ( τ ) ​ [ π ⁡ ( τ , p t ) − π ¯ ​ ( p t ) ] \frac{dp_{t}(\tau)}{dt}=p_{t}(\tau)\left[\pi(\tau,p_{t})-\bar{\pi}(p_{t})\right] (22) where [LaTeX: \pi(\tau,p_{t})] π ⁡ ( τ , p t ) \pi(\tau,p_{t}) is the payoff to type [LaTeX: \tau] τ \tau given population state [LaTeX: p_{t}] p t p_{t} , and [LaTeX: \bar{\pi}(p_{t})=\sum_{\tau^{\prime}}p_{t}(\tau^{\prime})\pi(\tau^{\prime},p_{t})] π ¯ ​ ( p t ) = ∑ τ ′ p t ​ ( τ ′ ) ​ π ​ ( τ ′ , p t ) \bar{\pi}(p_{t})=\sum_{\tau^{\prime}}p_{t}(\tau^{\prime})\pi(\tau^{\prime},p_{t}) is mean population payoff. Configurations with high legitimacy [LaTeX: L] L L and low friction [LaTeX: F] F F achieve higher survival probability; those with high stakes [LaTeX: \sigma] σ \sigma from supporting stakeholders achieve higher weight. Together, these determine which configurations persist. 4.2 Friction Dynamics The friction function (Eq. 6 ) characterizes tension at a point in time. Political reality is dynamic: stakes shift, alignments drift, information channels open and close. We develop the temporal dynamics of friction. 4.2.1 The Friction Equation From Definition 2.4 , friction in domain [LaTeX: d] d d at time [LaTeX: t] t t is: [LaTeX: F(d,t)=\sigma(d)\cdot\frac{1+\varepsilon(d,t)}{1+\alpha(d,t)}] F ⁡ ( d , t ) = σ ⁡ ( d ) ⋅ 1 + ε ⁡ ( d , t ) 1 + α ⁡ ( d , t ) F(d,t)=\sigma(d)\cdot\frac{1+\varepsilon(d,t)}{1+\alpha(d,t)} (29) Differentiating with respect to time: Proposition 4.2 (Friction Evolution) . This captures the legitimacy crisis that emerges when new stakeholders enter without corresponding voice. 4.4 Key Theorems We now establish the central theoretical results of the consent-friction framework. 4.4.1 Theorem: Consent-Holding Necessity Theorem 4.7 (Consent-Holding Necessity) . In any domain [LaTeX: d] d d where a non-null outcome obtains, there exists at least one agent [LaTeX: A] A A such that [LaTeX: A] A A holds consent over [LaTeX: d] d d . That is, consent-holding is a structural invariant of multi-agent coordination, not a contingent feature of particular arrangements. Proof. Suppose domain [LaTeX: d] d d produces outcome [LaTeX: o\neq\varnothing] o ≠ ∅ o\neq\varnothing . By the definition of domain, [LaTeX: d] d d is a locus of decision where actions affect outcomes. Since [LaTeX: o] o o obtains, some action [LaTeX: a] a a was executed (even “doing nothing” is an action with consequences). For action [LaTeX: a] a a to occur, some selection procedure [LaTeX: \pi] π \pi determined [LaTeX: a] a a from the space of possible actions [LaTeX: \mathcal{A}_{d}] 𝒜 d \mathcal{A}_{d} .
